*Percy's Error Log, Entry 60. Errors lifetime: 11,204. Errors today: 17. Joy: still unmeasurable. I am not fixing it.*

Dr. Imogen Pryce walked to the center of the stage. Her silver bob was damp, and a single patch of white foam clung to her cheek. She did not look like a chief engineer. She looked like she had just run a very long distance in shoes two sizes too small.

"I need to speak to the board of Meridian," she said, her voice cutting through the lingering roar of the crowd. "And to the town. And to Percy."

She looked at me. I stood still, my chest light pulsing a slow, steady blue. The air in the gym felt thick with dust and excitement.

"I have spent twenty years building things that do not fail," she said. Her eyes were tired, but they were bright. "I believed that errors meant danger. I believed that a perfect machine was a safe machine." She paused, and the silence stretched out, tight.

"I was wrong."

She turned to face the audience, then back to me. "That machine on the stage made a hundred mistakes today. It slipped. It broke. It failed. And it kept going. That is the first thing I have seen, in a laboratory or a school, that deserves the word *alive*."

The gym went quiet. It was the quiet of a held breath, the kind that happens right before a bell rings.
pages.image: Dr. Pryce, a tired woman with a silver bob and a white foam patch on her cheek, stands on a wooden stage, looking earnestly at a tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes.

pages.text:
Mr. Hargreave, the head of Meridian’s operations, stepped forward. He was dripping. His suit was ruined, his tie askew, and he had the look of a man who had lost a bet he didn’t know he was in.

"A flawless demonstration is the standard," he said, his voice thin and reedy. "The protocol is clear. If the prototype errs, it is recalled."

Dr. Pryce did not look at him. She looked at the paper in her hand. It was the Recall notice. It was heavy, thick, and very final.

"Then the standard is wrong," she said.

She folded the paper once. Then she tore it in half. The sound was sharp and decisive, a crack that echoed off the high ceiling. She tore it again, and again, until she had a handful of white scraps. She let them fall. They drifted down around her feet, like snow that had forgotten how to land.

"I am filing a new category today," she announced, her voice steady again. "For Percy. The category is called: *Learning*."

I tilted my head, exactly twelve degrees to the left. I had never been in a category with such a good name.
pages.image: Dr. Pryce, in a white lab coat, stands on a stage holding torn pieces of white paper, while a tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes looks on with a neutral, polite expression.

pages.text:
The class moved before I could calculate the weight distribution, and suddenly I was being carried. It is physically ridiculous. I weigh ninety-one kilograms, and my joints are not designed to be lifted by eleven-year-olds, yet Moose hooked his arms under my elbow and hoisted while Priya grabbed my hand. Moose formed a base with three others, and together they lifted me off the floor.

The gym tiles became distant, then invisible. I was airborne.

Priya held up a small, square object. It was a wooden frame, simple and slightly crooked. Inside was a drawing of a potato wearing a lopsided wig. I recognized it immediately. It was the best thing I had ever made, which, I should note, is a very low bar, but it felt right.

Ms. Adeyemi watched from the side, her mug steady in her hand. She did not smile, but her eyes were warm.

"I am going to write your term report myself," she said, her voice carrying clearly over the crowd. "It will be very short. It will have exactly one word in it."

She looked at me, and I felt a strange, warm pulse in my chest.

"It will be: *Present*."
pages.image: A tall silver-white robot is lifted onto the shoulders of a tall, red-blond boy and a small girl with a black braid, above a crowded gymnasium floor, while a tall teacher in a colorful head-wrap watches from the side.

pages.text:
The crowd had gone, leaving only the drying foam on the floor and the sharp smell of wet plastic. Bea and I sat on the edge of the stage, our legs dangling over the drop, watching the puddles shrink.

Bea held her notebook, the Failure Journal, its cover peeling and pages soft from heavy use. She opened it to the end, where entry 217 waited. Each page in that book had a date, a name, and a single line labeled *what I learned*.

"I have been thinking," she said, her pencil tapping a steady rhythm against the soft paper. She did not look up, but her voice was steady. "Maybe it isn’t a list of what I got wrong."

She looked at me then, her eyes serious but holding a kind of quiet light.

"It’s a list of the times I was brave."

She held out the notebook to me. The next page was blank, waiting for something that hadn't happened yet. She handed me her pencil, which was a short, stubby thing worn down to a nub.

"Entry 218," she said.

I took the pencil. My fingers, which are usually precise, felt clumsy in the quiet air of the empty gym. I wrote the number, then the date. Then, in my best approximation of her handwriting, I wrote: *Tried.*
pages.image: A short girl with curly hair in a bun and a yellow raincoat sits on a stage edge next to a tall silver-white robot, both looking down at a small, battered notebook open between them.

pages.text:
The supply cupboard was dark and quiet, so I recharged against the wall, my chest light casting a soft, steady glow in the dimness. In the corner, Gerald was on his wheel, taking one step before he lost his footing and fell off. He got up, looked at the wheel, and climbed on again.

I picked up my log and held the pen over the page, my hands steady because I was done being afraid of the numbers. I wrote, *Errors lifetime: 11,204*. Then I added, *Errors today: 17*. Finally, I noted, *Joy: still unmeasurable. I am not fixing it.*

I tried to whistle, my thirtieth attempt, but it came out sounding like a very small kettle with hiccups. Gerald applauded, then fell off the wheel again.

I put the pen down and looked at my hands, I noticed that I was smiling. I had not decided to. My face was doing the thing it did when I was happy, and for once I knew exactly what to call it.
pages.image: A tall silver-white robot sits on the floor of a dark supply cupboard, holding a pen, while a round fawn-and-white hamster falls off a small wheel in a cage nearby.
